Capital gains: compare annual sales with a final sale using after-tax values

Explore two invented realization schedules with the same starting capital, price appreciation and assumed tax on gains, then reconcile gross growth, tax payments and final spendable resources.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two invented gain-realization schedules after the assumed tax

Interactive planning lab

Annual realizations: ending value after modeled tax$144,504.39
Realize at final sale: ending value after modeled tax$147,167.1
Final sale minus annual after-tax endpoint$2,662.7

Two original non-registered capital-appreciation illustrations start with the same investment value and ACB and receive no new money. All return is assumed positive or zero price appreciation, with no distributions or other taxable events. In the annual case, all holdings are sold each year, that year’s gain is multiplied by the entered gain-tax fraction, tax is paid immediately from proceeds, and the remaining amount is reinvested as the new cost base. The final sale case makes no intervening disposition or distribution and pays modeled tax from the final sale proceeds. The same tax fraction applies to each full dollar of gain in both cases; it is not an inclusion rate, calculated personal marginal rate or actual assessment. No credits, deductions, loss rules, fees, trading spreads, registered accounts, deemed dispositions, special deferrals, foreign exchange, tax-rate changes or real payment deadlines are calculated. The appreciation and tax inputs are constant assumptions, not a product offer or forecast. Intermediate deferred-net points show hypothetical liquidation values, not taxes actually paid every year.

The central idea

The date tax leaves an investment can affect later compounding. Compare both cases after their remaining gain tax, and distinguish a larger tax bill from a smaller after-tax outcome.

01

Begin with the same capital and an explicitly limited return assumption

A tax-timing comparison can be distorted if one investment is shown before tax while another has already paid it. Start with the same resources, use consistent return assumptions and identify any tax still embedded in the ending market value before comparing the two outcomes.

This example places CAD 100,000 in each of two non-registered capital-appreciation scenarios. Opening adjusted cost base is also CAD 100,000. There are no new contributions, distributions, withdrawals for spending, fees or losses. Both holdings receive the same constant 5% annual price appreciation.

The independently selected tax assumption is 25% of each full dollar of realized gain. It is not a capital-gains inclusion rate or a personal marginal tax rate. The calculator neither combines those two concepts nor estimates a household’s actual tax. The assumption remains identical in both cases throughout the illustration.

02

Follow tax paid from each annual sale before reinvesting

The first case sells all its holdings at every year-end. It calculates that year’s gain relative to its current cost base, pays the assumed tax immediately from sale proceeds and reinvests the remainder. That reinvested amount becomes the new cost base for the following year.

In year one, CAD 100,000 grows to CAD 105,000. The CAD 5,000 gain produces CAD 1,250 of modeled tax, leaving CAD 103,750 invested. No extra household money pays that tax outside the scenario.

Year two therefore earns 5% on CAD 103,750, rather than on CAD 105,000. Its gain is CAD 5,187.50 and modeled tax is CAD 1,296.875 before rounding. The process continues for the selected horizon, with calculations retaining full precision.

At the default ten years, the annual-sale case ends with approximately CAD 144,504.39 after all its modeled gain taxes. The tax-payment dates are an arithmetic convention, rather than actual withholding or filing deadlines.

03

Deduct the accumulated gain tax from the final-sale case

The other case makes no intervening sale and receives no distribution or other taxable event under the stated assumptions. Its cost base remains CAD 100,000. Market value compounds at the full selected price-appreciation rate until the final sale.

After ten years, that market value is CAD 100,000 × 1.05 to the tenth power, or approximately CAD 162,889.46. Its remaining gain is CAD 62,889.46. Applying the same 25% assumption produces CAD 15,722.37 of modeled tax at liquidation.

The after-tax endpoint is approximately CAD 147,167.10, rather than the entire CAD 162,889.46 market value. It exceeds the annual-sale endpoint by about CAD 2,662.70 under these specific assumptions.

The waterfall taxes the gain, not the original capital. It adds gross appreciation to the initial cost and subtracts the modeled final tax once. The original principal is not subjected to that gain-tax fraction a second time.

04

Explain why the larger tax payment does not reverse this comparison

The annual-sale case earns approximately CAD 59,339.19 of cumulative gross appreciation on its changing invested balance. It pays approximately CAD 14,834.80 of modeled tax and retains CAD 44,504.39 of net growth.

The final-sale case earns more gross appreciation because its earlier gains remain invested without the intervening tax outflows. Its CAD 62,889.46 gross increase produces the larger CAD 15,722.37 tax payment, while still leaving the larger after-tax endpoint.

The grouped bars keep each case’s own gross growth, tax and net increase together. Within a row, net increase equals gross appreciation less modeled tax. Those three bars should not be added as separate sources of wealth.

Comparing only cumulative tax dollars would miss the additional growth. Comparing only gross market values would miss the remaining liability. Tax also occurs at different dates, so a simple total of payments is not a present-value measure of their cost.

05

Read intermediate liquidation values as valuations rather than repeated sales

The line chart shows the annual-sale balance, the final-sale case’s gross market balance and that same final-sale case’s hypothetical after-tax liquidation value at each completed year.

The last line asks what would remain if that position were sold at the indicated year. It does not pay all those intermediate hypothetical tax amounts and then pay them again at the selected finish. There is only one final sale in that scenario.

The matrix changes the holding horizon and the tax fraction for both cases together, while keeping initial capital and appreciation selected. One year produces no timing difference because both cases sell at the same date. A zero tax assumption or zero appreciation also removes the modeled advantage.

The cells do not assign probabilities to returns or identify a future tax rate. A longer horizon magnifies the effect of constant compounding in the illustration, while real returns, laws, cash needs and portfolio choices can change during that time.

06

Keep actual taxable events and investment decisions outside the shortcut

The CRA’s Capital Gains guide explains that a gain or loss usually arises when capital property is sold or considered sold. This article does not model deemed dispositions, reserves, exemptions or other special treatment. It uses the general gain concept with original hypothetical tax inputs.

Holding a fund without selling its units does not establish that every return can remain untaxed until a final sale. The CRA’s mutual-fund guidance discusses distributions while a holding is owned, including reinvested amounts. Those events and their cost-base adjustments are deliberately absent here.

Reconcile actual income categories, transactions, cost records and payment dates before estimating a real after-tax goal amount. Investment suitability, diversification, fees and the need to sell can matter independently of this timing effect. The comparison isolates one mechanism; it does not determine whether postponing a particular sale is appropriate.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical charts assume all return is nonnegative capital appreciation, no distributions and one constant tax fraction on realized gains. They do not calculate a statutory inclusion rate, personal tax, trading recommendation or available product return. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. CRA · Capital Gains, guide T4037 ↗

    2025-return guide reviewed 25 October 2026 for general disposition and capital-gain calculation context. No published inclusion rate, deduction or personal tax result is imported. The model uses an independent constant tax fraction on the full realized gain and invented payment dates.

  2. CRA · Tax treatment of mutual funds ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for the distinction between fund distributions and gains on selling units. Actual distributions, their tax character and ACB adjustments are excluded from this pure-price-appreciation illustration.
